# Welcome {#sec-welcome .unnumbered}

<!-- This landing page will contain an image -->
<!-- and a short text about the reasoning behind the book and what it is trying to achieve. -->

This book takes a developmental approach to visualization
motivating each new principle and chart element
as a response to a limitation of what came before.
The aim is to try to clearly visualize the underlying need
rather than just learning rules of which charts are good for what.
This is because I have noticed that learners
can be apt at remembering that
they should use one chart instead of another
without understanding why that's the case.
Or they might understand why for a specific example,
but not be able to generalize that understanding further.

I consider that helping learners understand and generalize
is a way to empower their agency
and improve their ability to predict
what is an effective visualization choice
for a visualization not previously encountered .
At least it is my hope
that this book can contribute to and encourage
readers' critical thinking about any chart they might come across.
In my experience, this angle also makes learning more fun.

This books interleaves exercises throughout the chapters
to encourage experiential learning
and ignite readers intuition and make their learning more active.
The exercises are largely focused on visualization principles
rather than coding,
since memorization of library APIs
is an increasingly replaceable skill;
although understanding the guiding principles
of how those APIs are designed
can be informative
(e.g. the rules of a grammar of graphics library).

To make the learning interactive,
the book also include code in a few libraries
that implements a version of the grammar of graphics.
I focus on these
because I think they empower student
in a similar way as described above:
the predictable grammar encourages learners to interpolate
what **could** work based on understanding the rules of the grammar.
